title: HashSet patterns
summary: Instant membership tests: remove duplicates and solve two-sum in one pass.

steps.title: A set answers "have I seen this?"
body: `HashSet<T>` is a hash table with keys and no values. Its superpower is `Contains` in **O(1)** on average, where `List<T>.Contains` scans every item.

`Add` returns `false` when the item was already present, which makes de-duplication a one-liner inside a loop. Watch `seen` fill up while `result` keeps only first appearances, in their original order.

code: foreach (var w in "the cat saw the other cat".Split(' '))
steps.explain: `the` and `cat` each appear twice. Their second `Add` returns `false`.

steps.prompt: You check 100,000 items, one by one, against a collection of 100,000 others. Roughly how many steps with a `List<int>` versus a `HashSet<int>`?
steps.explain: `List.Contains` is `O(n)`, so `n` lookups cost `O(n²)`. `HashSet.Contains` is `O(1)` on average, so the whole job is `O(n)`.

steps.title: Two-sum in one pass
body: **Two-sum**: do any two numbers in the array add up to `target`? Checking every pair is `O(n²)`.
Turn it around: when you reach `x`, the partner you need is `target - x`. If that partner is already in a set of earlier numbers, you are done. Otherwise remember `x` and move on. One pass, `O(n)`.
Watch `need` and `seen` as the loop runs with `target = 13`.

steps.prompt: Same loop with `target = 7`. What does it print?
steps.explain: Nothing matches until `x = 2`, whose partner `5` is already in the set. The pair is found when its **second** number arrives.

steps.prompt: Two-sum returning **indexes**: a `Dictionary` remembers where each earlier number was.
code: if (indexOf.TryGetValue(__1__, out var j)) return new[] { __2__, i };
steps.explain: The key is the value, the stored item is its index. Adding `a[i]` *after* the check stops a number pairing with itself.

steps.prompt: Match each `HashSet` method to what it leaves in `a`, starting from `a = {1, 2, 3}` and `b = {2, 3, 4}`.

steps.title: Dedupe and two-sum
prompt: - `int[] Dedupe(int[] a)`: the distinct values in order of first appearance. `{ 4, 2, 4, 7, 2 }` gives `{ 4, 2, 7 }`.
- `int[] TwoSum(int[] a, int target)`: indexes `{ i, j }` with `i < j` and `a[i] + a[j] == target`, choosing the pair whose **`j` is smallest**; an empty array if there is none.
The tests use 200,000 numbers, so nested loops will run out of time. Do not use `Distinct()`.
solution: if (indexOf.TryGetValue(target - a[i], out var j)) return new[] { j, i };
template: Dojo.Eq("Dedupe keeps first appearances", new[] { 4, 2, 7 }, Dedupe(new[] { 4, 2, 4, 7, 2 }));
Dojo.Eq("Dedupe of an empty array", new int[0], Dedupe(new int[0]));
Dojo.Eq("TwoSum with no answer is empty", new int[0], TwoSum(new[] { 1, 2, 3 }, 100));
Dojo.Eq("a number cannot pair with itself", new int[0], TwoSum(new[] { 4 }, 8));
Dojo.Eq("but two equal numbers can", new[] { 0, 2 }, TwoSum(new[] { 4, 1, 4 }, 8));
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI < dojoBig.Length; dojoI++) dojoBig[dojoI] = dojoI * 2;
Dojo.Eq("200,000 numbers: Dedupe is fast", 200_000, Dedupe(dojoBig).Length);
Dojo.Eq("200,000 numbers: TwoSum is fast", new[] { 199_998, 199_999 }, TwoSum(dojoBig, 799_994));
hints: TwoSum: a `Dictionary<int, int>` from value to index. Check `target - a[i]` before storing `a[i]`.
